content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated recommendations regarding the use of tranexamic acid (TXA) for the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). PPH is defined as a blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours after childbirth and affects approximately 5% of women globally. It is a leading cause of maternal mortality, particularly in low-income countries, where it accounts for nearly one-quarter of all maternal deaths. Addressing PPH is critical to improving maternal health outcomes and achieving the health targets of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The updated WHO recommendation emphasizes the early use of intravenous TXA, administered within three hours of childbirth, in addition to standard care, for women diagnosed with PPH following vaginal or cesarean delivery. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence and is strongly supported by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The recommended dosage is 1 gram of TXA administered intravenously over 10 minutes, with a second dose of 1 gram if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours of the initial dose. The evidence indicates that TXA administration beyond three hours after birth does not provide clinical benefits and may even pose potential harm. The recommendation applies to all cases of PPH, regardless of the cause, including bleeding due to genital tract trauma or other factors. However, TXA should not be used in women with known contraindications, such as a history of thromboembolic events during pregnancy. The updated recommendation supersedes the 2012 WHO guidance on TXA for PPH treatment. It reflects new evidence, including findings from the WOMAN trial, a large randomized controlled trial that demonstrated the effectiveness of early TXA administration in reducing mortality and morbidity associated with PPH. The primary audience for this recommendation includes healthcare professionals involved in developing national and local health protocols, as well as those providing direct care to women during childbirth, such as midwives, nurses, general practitioners, obstetricians, and maternal health program managers. It is also relevant to policymakers, professional societies, and organizations promoting maternal health. The recommendation was developed using WHO's standardized guideline development procedures, which include identifying priority questions, synthesizing evidence using the GRADE methodology, and consulting an international group of experts. The process involved contributions from the WHO Steering Group, the Guideline Development Group, external reviewers, and systematic review teams. The recommendation aims to support the global implementation of TXA as part of comprehensive PPH management strategies, ultimately reducing maternal mortality and morbidity worldwide.
